Goals

  • Use facet functions to create separate, related plots for different groups
  • See Simpson’s Paradox in a data set
  • See some options for visualizing groups in a data set

Setup

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(palmerpenguins)

Data files

This assignment uses the NMH dataset. Download the NMH data folder from Canvas and put it as a subdirectory of your working directory. It assumes that the data files are in a subdirectory of the working directory called NHM. Adjust your working directory if needed; do not change the file paths in the code below, or the instructor will not be able to knit your file.

stays <- read_csv("NMH/stays.csv")

Simpson’s Paradox

When data is aggregated across groups, the relationship between variables in the aggregated data can be different than the relationship between variables within each group individually. This is one reason it is critical to include categorical variables in data visualizations and examine within-group patterns.

We can see an example of this situation with data on penguins from the palmerpenguins package.

penguins
## # A tibble: 344 × 8
##    species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_…¹ body_…² sex    year
##    <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>      <int>   <int> <fct> <int>
##  1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7        181    3750 male   2007
##  2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4        186    3800 fema…  2007
##  3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18          195    3250 fema…  2007
##  4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA           NA      NA <NA>   2007
##  5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3        193    3450 fema…  2007
##  6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6        190    3650 male   2007
##  7 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8        181    3625 fema…  2007
##  8 Adelie  Torgersen           39.2          19.6        195    4675 male   2007
##  9 Adelie  Torgersen           34.1          18.1        193    3475 <NA>   2007
## 10 Adelie  Torgersen           42            20.2        190    4250 <NA>   2007
## # … with 334 more rows, and abbreviated variable names ¹​flipper_length_mm,
## #   ²​body_mass_g

Make a plot of penguins’ bill depth vs. bill length, and include a trend line:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=bill_length_mm,
                     y=bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method="lm")  # linear regression fit

Hmm, this seems off – penguins with longer bills have flatter bills? It’s possible, but usually two size measurements of an animal would be at least weakly positively correlated.

Looking at the plot, the overall trend may also seem to not quite fit – there are some clusters where it seems like there is a positive correlation between these variables. While visual impressions can be misleading (people have a tendency to see patterns where they may not exist), this is worth investigating further.

So let’s look at the data by species:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=bill_length_mm,
                     y=bill_depth_mm,
                     color=species)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method="lm")  # linear regression fit

Ahh - the completely opposite relationship! This is what we’re talking about – when the relationship within each group (all of the groups here!) is one direction, but the overall relationship between the variables is different.

Facets

Facet functions allow you to make multiple small, related plots. While you can use the facet functions to make various kinds of small multiple plots, by default, the facet functions in ggplot2 are designed to help you make the same plot (same scales, same variable mappings, same geoms) for non-overlapping subsets of the data, defined by a categorical variable. This means you define the overall plot as you normally would, but when you add a facet function, instead of making just one plot, it makes one plot per group.

There are two different facet functions: facet_wrap and facet_grid. While you can control the layout of facets with either function, as a rule of thumb, use facet_wrap when you have many groups and a single grouping variable you want to facet with, and use facet_grid if you want to facet by two variables or you want to control the layout of the facets.

Functionally, facet_wrap computes the different facets (possibly by crossing 2 or more grouping variables) then lays them all out, while facet_grid uses the grouping variables to structure the layout – it draw the structure, then fills in the facets. This difference is reflected in the how the facet labels are shown by default.

Example

Look at how many times a patient’s glucose is tested per day.

stays %>%
  ggplot(aes(avg_tests_day)) +
  # choose bins of width .5 (half day) that run 0-.5, .5-1, etc.
  geom_histogram(binwidth=.5, center=0.25) + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,15))  # limit the range (there are some outliers)

There are two peaks in the distribution. Let’s try to figure this out.

One partial explanation for the variation may be whether a patient is taking insulin; we can examine this with a faceted plot:

stays %>%
  ggplot(aes(avg_tests_day)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=.5, center=0.25) + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,15)) +  # limit the range (there are some outliers)
  # above lines are the same as the overall plot in the chunk above
  # then facet:
  facet_grid(insulin ~ .)

Here, we’re using facet_grid because insulin has only two groups and we want to control the layout of the facets. The formula syntax used by the function allows us to specify that we want insulin groups laid out along the y-axis (y ~ x) – vertically. The . indicates there’s no variable to facet along the x-axis (horizontally).

We want to lay out the facets vertically because we want to compare the two plots based on where values are on the x-axis. When we lay out the plots vertically, they will all share a single x-axis. If we lay them out horizontally, it is much harder to tell that the second non-insulin peak aligns with the insulin-taking peak:

stays %>%
  ggplot(aes(avg_tests_day)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=.5, center=0.25) + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,15)) + 
  facet_grid(~ insulin)

This alignment makes it clearer that there are more insulin-takers in the data though. Facet layout should be chosen depending on what you want to compare.

For patients who are taking insulin, the distribution of number of glucose tests per day is roughly normal. For patients not taking glucose, there are still two groups - a lower number of average tests per day, and an average number of tests per day that is more similar to patients taking insulin.

See how the faceted plot above compares to the same plot using color to distinguish the groups instead of facets:

stays %>%
  ggplot(aes(avg_tests_day, fill=insulin)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=.5, center=0.25) + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,15))

Here, we can see that the small peak on the left (lower values of avg_tests_day) is mostly those who don’t take insulin, but it’s harder to see what’s going on for the more typical range of values (4+).

EXERCISE 1

Make a histogram of age. Make the bins width 5, running from 0-5, 5-10, etc. Then facet the plot by admit_type. Align the facets so they are stacked on top of each other (single column).

Bonus: get the facet labels on the top of each plot instead of on the side to make them easier to read.

stays %>%
  ggplot(aes(age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=5, center=0.25)+
  facet_wrap(~admit_type, ncol = 1)

Facet Scales

The default with facets is for all small plots to share the same x and y scales, including the ranges. This is a good default because it allows the viewer of a plot to use position within the plot grid to make inferences and comparisons more easily.

This default behavior can be changed, however, to allow the scale limits on each small plot to be computed independently – to “free” the x and/or y scale.

EXERCISE 2

  1. Look up how to free the axis scales in a faceted plot. Edit the plot you made in Exercise 1 so that the limits on the y-axis can vary for each facet.

  2. Do you find the original or the new plot to be more useful if you are trying to compare the proportion of younger patients for each admit type?

stays %>%
  ggplot(aes(age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=5, center=0.25)+
  facet_wrap(~admit_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1)

The graph made in question 1 is more readable in terms of comparing the age distribution by admit_type. But it would be more interesting to make the new graph when we are looking for more precise information on each category.

Adding Summary Measures

Sometimes it’s useful to add indicators of summary statistics such as means or medians to a plot. This can be a little tricky to do with facets.

Let’s add a vertical line at the median value. We want the median for each facet separately.

If we add geom_vline() and try to compute the median within aes(), we get the overall median put on all of the plots (not what we want):

stays %>%
  ggplot(aes(mean_glucose)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=50) + 
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept=median(mean_glucose)), color="red") +
  facet_grid(admit_type ~ .)

The most straightforward way is to compute the median for each group ahead of time, stored in a separate data frame, and supply that to geom_vline()

# create a data frame that has our facetting variable, and 
# then the values we need (here a single one) for the geom 
# we want to add in each facet
medians <- stays %>% 
  group_by(admit_type) %>%
  summarize(med=median(mean_glucose))
medians
## # A tibble: 5 × 2
##   admit_type          med
##   <chr>             <dbl>
## 1 Direct Admit       162.
## 2 Elective           153.
## 3 Emergency          162.
## 4 External Transfer  161.
## 5 Urgent             154.
stays %>%
  ggplot(aes(mean_glucose)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=50) + 
  # admit_type is in medians, so it knows how to map to the facets
  geom_vline(data=medians,  # the data frame we made
             aes(xintercept=med), # med is a column in medians
             color="red") +
  facet_grid(admit_type ~ .)

EXERCISE 3

Make a plot showing the distribution of stay_length for each age_decade of patient age (a histogram for each age_decade). Add the median value for each age_decade to the plot.

Limit the range of the x-axis to where the bulk of the data is so that you can see any differences in the medians by group (exclude outliers with very long stay lengths).

Choose an appropriate binwidth for the histograms.

Remember: you may need to increase the fig.height chunk option to make the plot readable in the html output when you knit.

stays <- mutate(stays, 
                age_decade = case_when(age < 20 ~ "Teens",
                                       age < 30 ~ "20s",
                                       age < 40 ~ "30s",
                                       age < 50 ~ "40s",
                                       age < 60 ~ "50s",
                                       age < 70 ~ "60s",
                                       age < 80 ~ "70s",
                                       TRUE ~ "80s"),
                age_decade = factor(age_decade, 
                                    levels=c("Teens", "20s", "30s", "40s", "50s", "60s", "70s", "80s")))
medians <- stays %>% 
  group_by(age_decade) %>%
  summarize(med=median(stay_length))
medians
## # A tibble: 8 × 2
##   age_decade   med
##   <fct>      <dbl>
## 1 Teens       4.19
## 2 20s         3.87
## 3 30s         3.99
## 4 40s         4.25
## 5 50s         4.9 
## 6 60s         4.67
## 7 70s         4.89
## 8 80s         5.24
stays %>%
  ggplot(aes(stay_length)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=40) + 
  # admit_type is in medians, so it knows how to map to the facets
  geom_vline(data=medians,  # the data frame we made
             aes(xintercept=med), # med is a column in medians
             color="red") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,30)) +
  facet_grid(age_decade ~ .)
